content: A menstrual disorder refers to any irregularity in a woman's menstrual cycle. Oligoovulation is the term used to describe infrequent or irregular ovulation, typically defined as menstrual cycles that are 36 days or longer, or fewer than 8 cycles per year. Anovulation is the absence of ovulation during a time when it would normally be expected, such as in a post-menarcheal, premenopausal woman. This condition often presents as irregular menstrual periods, characterized by unpredictable variability in the intervals, duration, or amount of bleeding. Anovulation can also lead to the cessation of menstrual periods (secondary amenorrhea) or excessive uterine bleeding (dysfunctional uterine bleeding). Polymenorrhea is the medical term for abnormally frequent menstruation, where the cycle interval is less than 21 days. Despite the increased frequency, the quantity and duration of bleeding are typically normal. Differential Diagnosis for menstrual irregularities includes causes such as anovulatory cycles, biphasic cycles, and hyperthyroidism. Drug Causes of menstrual irregularities may include medications such as misoprostol and valdecoxib. Oligomenorrhea refers to infrequent or light menstrual periods, with a cycle frequency exceeding 35 days. Dysmenorrhea, also known as painful menstruation, involves menstrual periods accompanied by either sharp, intermittent pain or dull, aching pain, usually localized to the pelvis or lower abdomen. Amenorrhea is the absence of menstrual periods in a woman of reproductive age. Physiological states of amenorrhea occur during pregnancy and lactation (breastfeeding). Outside of the reproductive years, amenorrhea is normal during childhood and after menopause. Menorrhagia is characterized by abnormally heavy and prolonged menstrual bleeding. The underlying causes may include abnormal blood clotting, disruptions in the hormonal regulation of the menstrual cycle, or disorders affecting the endometrial lining of the uterus. Depending on the cause, menorrhagia may also be associated with abnormally painful periods (dysmenorrhea).
